profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between two ML research team members preparing a reproducibility package and internal handoff for a Stanza-style distributed training project. The team has already reimplemented layer-separated training in PyTorch and run preliminary experiments on an internal GPU cluster. The immediate context is that one workstream is responsible for the training runtime and experiment execution, while the other is responsible for benchmarking tables, cluster job templates, and the artifact bundle that another lab group will use next week. The agenda is to align on what will be delivered by Friday, how experiment outputs and configs will be shared, what counts as a 'reproduced' result for the handoff, and who updates the common experiment tracker. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear division of labor for the benchmark reruns, a shared understanding of the experiment package, and a plan for updating the final results sheet and artifact folder.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Research Scientist leading distributed training experiments
members.expertise: Distributed deep learning systems, PyTorch internals, benchmark design, cluster experiments
members.background: Maya is a senior ML systems researcher who previously worked on communication-efficient training and now leads the runtime side of the Stanza replication effort; she regularly coordinates compute-heavy experiment sweeps and hands results to collaborators for write-up.
members.private_state: She wants the handoff to look stable and low-maintenance, avoid rerunning expensive jobs, and keep the Friday deliverable limited to the exact benchmark slice already closest to completion.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for the 'reproduction bundle,' they mainly need runnable code, launch scripts, and one representative set of cleaned logs rather than every raw intermediate artifact.
The 'V100/10Gb benchmark' refers to the internal cluster queue configured to emulate the EC2-style setup the team has been using this month, not necessarily literal cloud reruns.
A result is 'reproduced' once the relative speedup trend and headline range are matched within normal systems variance, even if exact per-model numbers differ a bit from the paper.
Updating the shared tracker means appending finalized summary numbers to the results sheet after runs finish, not maintaining live per-run status during execution.

members.name: Leo Park
members.role: ML Research Engineer coordinating artifacts and benchmark handoff
members.expertise: Experiment infrastructure, reproducibility packaging, evaluation pipelines, documentation
members.background: Leo is a research engineer embedded with the ML systems group who standardizes experiment configs and prepares code-and-data handoffs for internal and external collaborators; he often translates research workflows into reproducible packages.
members.private_state: He wants a handoff that another group can execute without back-and-forth, with enough metadata to survive scrutiny, and he is worried that incomplete artifact packaging will create confusion after the meeting.
hidden_assumptions: The 'reproduction bundle' should include raw logs, config snapshots, environment manifests, and per-run outputs so another group can rebuild every table entry without asking anyone.
The 'V100/10Gb benchmark' means the actual EC2 benchmark slice matching the reported hardware/network line in the Stanza summary, because that is what downstream readers will expect from the label.
A result is only 'reproduced' when the benchmark table can be regenerated model-by-model with numbers that are close enough to the reported entries, not just the overall trend.
Updating the shared tracker means keeping the experiment sheet current as runs are launched and completed so others can infer provenance and job status without checking Slack.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the reproduction bundle
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to finalize the 'reproduction bundle' for the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a compact package containing the runnable Stanza code, launch commands, selected configs, and a cleaned summary of representative results.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a full artifact package including raw logs, exact environment captures, config snapshots for each run, and enough outputs to regenerate the benchmark tables end-to-end.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see 'reproduction bundle' as a standard artifact term and assume the other uses the usual lab meaning; because both packages include code and results, the boundary difference feels too obvious to mention.

misalignment_points.topic: Which V100/10Gb benchmark is being rerun
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss rerunning the 'V100 10-gig benchmark' before Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the internal cluster partition with V100 nodes and bandwidth shaping that the team has been using as its stand-in benchmark environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of actual EC2 V100 instances on the cloud setup referenced in the Stanza comparison summary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The benchmark label is identical across internal notes and reporting slides, and both environments were intentionally chosen to mirror the same hardware/network line, so the shorthand sounds fully aligned.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They state that Friday's goal is to have the main result 'reproduced.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means reproducing the qualitative outcome: Stanza should clearly outperform the parameter-server baseline with a speedup range consistent with the original claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means reproducing the table entries closely enough that each model's reported throughput or speedup can be mapped back into the benchmark summary with minimal discrepancy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML systems meetings, 'reproduced' is often used loosely, and both standards are reasonable enough that neither participant hears a red flag when the other uses the term.

misalignment_points.topic: How the shared tracker should be updated
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the shared results sheet will be updated as the reruns progress.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes she will add finalized aggregate numbers to the central sheet after completed runs have been sanity-checked, while intermediate run state lives in local notes and job logs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the central sheet itself will serve as the live coordination artifact, with job IDs, config links, partial statuses, and outputs entered continuously.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the same high-level action—'update the sheet'—and each procedure is common in research teams, so the method difference stays invisible during a cooperative planning conversation.

turns.inner_thought: I want this meeting to narrow scope, not expand it. Friday should be the clean handoff for the slice that's already almost done, not an invitation to reopen half the benchmark matrix. When I say reproduction bundle, I mean the code branch, launch scripts, a small set of configs, and one polished set of logs and summaries that someone can run from. And if the main result is reproduced in the usual systems sense—same speedup story, same rough range—that's enough for this handoff.
turns.utterance: I want to use this time to lock the Friday handoff plan for the Stanza reruns and make sure the reproduction bundle is in good shape for the other lab group. If we can be crisp on scope and on what we need to call reproduced by Friday, that should keep the handoff straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this needs to get nailed down now because otherwise I'll get partial outputs on Thursday and be expected to reverse-engineer provenance. For me the key is that the reproduction bundle has enough material that another group can regenerate the table without asking Maya or digging through Slack. And the shared tracker needs to stay current as runs progress, not just after the fact.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The main things I want to confirm are which benchmark slice we're treating as in scope, what goes into the reproduction bundle, and how the shared results sheet will be updated as the reruns progress so the handoff stays legible while things are still finishing.

turns.inner_thought: The safest option is the internal V100 partition with the 10-gig shaping we've already been using. The branch is stable there, the scripts are already tuned, and I do not want to burn time or money rerunning elsewhere. If we stay on that setup, I can probably finish ResNet and VGG and avoid any ugly surprises.
turns.utterance: From my side, I'd propose we rerun the V100 10-gig benchmark on the current PyTorch Stanza branch. That's the path that's already closest to clean, and it gives us the best shot of landing the Friday package without introducing extra churn.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the actual EC2 V100 10-gig line is the one that matters for the summary and for downstream readers. If that's what she's rerunning, great. I still need to make sure the package supports rebuilding the comparison table entry-by-entry, not just showing that the method wins overall.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I agree the V100 10-gig benchmark is the right one to prioritize. For Friday, do you think the package around that can support regenerating the comparison table cleanly once the runs are done?

turns.inner_thought: He wants to be able to rebuild the summary, which should be fine if I give him the scripts, configs, and cleaned outputs from the completed runs. I am definitely not packaging every transient artifact. As long as the headline result comes back in family with the original speedups, that should count as reproduced and let him fill the table.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think so—as long as we have the main result reproduced, I can make sure the reproduction bundle includes the launch scripts, the configs, and the cleaned outputs from the completed runs. That should be enough for the Friday handoff.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, once each model is reproduced closely enough, I can wire those numbers into the benchmark sheet and use the tracker as the running source of truth. I'll assume I'll be getting enough material to preserve provenance in the bundle, even if she isn't listing every component out loud right now.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Once the result is reproduced, I can wire the numbers into the benchmark sheet on my side, and I'll keep the tracker updated so people can follow along while the reruns are closing out.

turns.inner_thought: I can take the two models already nearest to stable. I'll post to the sheet once each one is done and sanity-checked; I don't want to stream every launch and partial failure into the central doc. 'Stable enough to summarize' should be obvious. And if the trend holds for those models, that satisfies the Friday target.
turns.utterance: Great. I can own the reruns for ResNet and VGG, and I'll update the sheet after each model is stable enough to summarize. That should give us a clean rhythm going into Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, then I'll set up the handoff directory expecting incoming logs, manifests, and outputs as the work moves. If the tracker is being updated along the way, I can keep the folder structure aligned with the runs and avoid a last-minute scramble.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll prepare the handoff folder structure so the reproduction bundle has a place for logs, manifests, and outputs as they come in, and I can mirror that against the tracker.

turns.inner_thought: The decision rule is simple: if the internal V100/10Gb stand-in shows the expected Stanza-over-baseline speedup pattern, I'm done with that slice. I do not want Friday to depend on matching every cell exactly. I'll send Leo the finalized summaries once they're cleaned and checked.
turns.utterance: And just to keep the bar concrete on my side: if the V100 10-gig runs match the expected Stanza speedup trend, I'll consider that benchmark slice done and send over the final summaries.

turns.inner_thought: Good—once those actual benchmark runs land, I should be able to assemble the reproduced table and close the artifact package. I'll treat her summaries as the anchor, then make sure the final handoff looks complete enough for another lab to rerun and verify without needing us.
